title: Convergence to the exact kinetics of the one-dimensional Riviera model
abstract: The Riviera model is a random sequential deposition model for house building on a lattice, in which a house cannot be built when both nearest-neighbor sites are already occupied. In one dimension, an attempted deposition is therefore rejected whenever the target site is an isolated vacancy. Despite the apparent simplicity of this rule, no exact analytical solution of the original model is currently known. We derive an infinite hierarchy of kinetic equations governing its dynamics and introduce a systematic closure scheme that can be implemented at arbitrary finite order. Solving the resulting systems order by order, we show that the corresponding kinetics converges rapidly toward the exact behavior. At high order, the method yields an exceptionally accurate estimate of the jamming density while retaining explicit analytical expressions for the full time-dependent evolution.
summary: This paper tackles the complex kinetics of the 1D Riviera model by developing a powerful mathematical technique: solving an infinite hierarchy of kinetic equations through systematic, order-by-order truncation. The method successfully provides highly accurate analytical estimates for both the final jamming density and the full time evolution of site occupation probabilities.
main_problem: The primary challenge is determining the exact kinetics of the one-dimensional Riviera model, which involves long-range dynamical correlations preventing a finite analytical solution.
main_result: The authors developed a systematic closure scheme for an infinite hierarchy of kinetic equations, demonstrating that increasing the truncation order leads to rapid and highly accurate convergence toward the true physical behavior.
method: They derived an infinite hierarchy of coupled differential equations governing joint occupation probabilities and systematically truncated this hierarchy at arbitrary finite orders using mean-field approximations for long-range correlations.
model_or_system: The system is the one-dimensional Riviera model, a random sequential deposition process on a lattice where site occupancy depends on nearest-neighbor availability (i.e., isolated vacancies cannot be filled).
key_observables: Occupation probabilities ($\pi_0, \pi_m, \pi_d, \pi_1$), the jamming density ($\pi_1(\infty)$), and the full time-dependent evolution of these densities.
important_parameters: The truncation order ($l$) of the kinetic hierarchy; the final jamming density $\pi_1(\infty)$.
main_assumptions: The core approximation involves replacing higher-order joint probabilities with a specific mean-field exponential form, which allows for the solvability of the truncated linear system.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the convergence of key probabilities ($p_{000}(t)$, $p_{0010}(t)$) across different approximation orders (e.g., 10th vs. 22nd). Figure 5 shows the nonmonotonic time evolution of monomer and dimer densities.
paper_structure: The paper builds by first establishing the infinite hierarchy, then systematically applying closures at increasing orders (first, second, up to twenty-second), presenting results for observables like jamming density convergence and full time-dependent analytical expressions derived from these truncated systems.
why_interesting: While focused on classical statistical mechanics, the method of deriving an infinite hierarchy and using systematic closure schemes is mathematically analogous to techniques used in quantum field theory or open quantum system dynamics where exact solutions are intractable.

Figure 2. Semilogarithmic plot of the time evolution of p000(t) (left) and p0010(t) (right) for the first three approximation orders.

Figure 2 compares the first three approximation orders for the key quantities p000(t) and p0010(t). Relative to the first-order results, the third-order probabilities display significant long-time corrections, and both decay as e−t. (Note that the two first orders of p0010(t) are identical). Their convergence is expected to improve rapidly as probabilities associated with longer intervals are incorporated.

Figure 3. Semilogarithmic plot of the time evolution of p000(t) (top left) and p0010(t) (top right) for the 10, 15 and 22nd-order approximations. The absolute difference ∆p1 = |p(10) −p(15)| and ∆p2 = |p(15) −p(22)| shows the convergence of the method for p000 (bottom left) and p0010 (bottom right).
